title: HIS-201 Ch. 5 — 1 Definitions
subject: HIS-201
topic: Chapter 5: The Mosaic of Eighteenth-Century America

cards.def: A Spanish military garrison, the defensive outpost that held a frontier region such as Texas or California alongside the missions.
A Franciscan community meant to gather Indians into an orderly, regimented life, shielded from outside influence, and teach them to be "industrious and devout."
Sums of money a bride brought to her marriage, meant to help the young couple get established.
A widow's own clothes, jewelry and similar personal items, which English law let her keep.
The French "upper country": the Great Lakes, north to Lakes Manitoba and Winnipeg, and south along the Mississippi basin.
A scholar's term for the creative compromises the French and Indians worked out when their customs, especially their laws, clashed.
The colonial fighting, with Indian allies on both sides, of the European war in which England joined the Netherlands and the League of Augsburg against France.
The second colonial war between England and France and their Indian allies, the American side of the War of the Spanish Succession.
Population growth that comes from births outnumbering deaths, rather than from immigration.
Contracts to work as a servant in America for a set term in order to pay for the Atlantic passage.
The cramped, airless between-decks "upper hold" where poor passengers and servants crossed the Atlantic.
The frontier region west of the settled seaboard, from western Pennsylvania south into Virginia and the Carolinas.
A northern seaport festival in which black residents paraded in their masters' clothes and elected their own "kings, governors, and judges" to settle minor disputes.
Forcing colonial men into service in the British navy, usually by "press gangs."
A rice-country labor system in which each slave worked an assigned daily task, after which the master felt no right to call on him.
Settlements of runaway slaves, usually recently arrived Africans who fled inland together.
Everyday quiet resistance by slaves, such as faking illness, feigning stupidity or laziness, breaking tools, pilfering and hiding in the woods.
An intellectual movement that started in Europe in the 1600s and stressed the power of human reason to promote progress by revealing the laws that governed nature and society.
The fixed laws governing nature and society that Enlightenment thinkers believed human reason could discover.
The belief that events happen by God's direct will, the traditional explanation of the world that most colonists kept instead of natural law.
An Enlightenment-inspired faith in a benevolent God who offers salvation to everyone, with reason as God's greatest gift for following Jesus's moral teachings.
A belief that rejected the divinity of Jesus and looked to nature rather than the Bible, seeing God as a "Supreme Architect" who made the world and withdrew, leaving natural law.
The mid-1700s religious revival whose emotional preaching called on people to experience a "new birth" through conversion.
Preaching that stresses the need for a "new birth" through religious conversion.
Traveling ministers who preached wherever crowds gathered rather than serving one church.
Lay people, including women and enslaved or common black people, preaching to any audience that would listen.
The surge in demand for British-made goods that let people of ordinary means own small luxuries like tea, gloves and soap.
The middle class of people of moderate means, between the rich and the struggling poor.
England's government in theory, balancing the Crown (monarchy), the House of Lords (aristocracy) and the House of Commons (the people).
Rewarding supporters with government offices and contracts to buy their loyalty.
A lawmaking body with two houses, here an elected lower house or assembly and an upper house or council.
The book's term for Britain's loose, hands-off rule of its colonies before 1760, which left colonists a great deal of freedom.
